read.bigIdea: Whiskey is grain, aged in oak.
read.where: Whiskey is distilled from a **grain mash** and aged in **oak**. The grain sets the style: corn, rye, wheat or malted barley. Time in the barrel adds **color** and flavors like **vanilla** and spice, and softens the spirit. In the US, whiskey is bottled at **80 proof or more**.
read.visualIntro: In the US, the grain names the whiskey:
read.mixup: **Whiskey** is the family. **Bourbon**, **rye** and **Scotch** are kinds of whiskey.
read.sayIt: Do you like it sweeter, like a bourbon, or spicier, like a rye?

in the US can make bourbon, not only Kentucky.

whiskey is filtered through maple charcoal first.

read.bigIdea: Corn is sweeter; rye is spicier.
read.where: **Bourbon** is American whiskey of at least **51% corn**, aged in **new charred oak**. It can be made **anywhere in the US**, not only Kentucky. Corn makes it rounder and **sweeter**: vanilla and caramel. **Rye whiskey** is at least **51% rye**, so it’s **drier and spicier**. **Wheated** bourbons swap rye for wheat and taste softer. **Tennessee whiskey**, like Jack Daniel’s, follows the bourbon rules and is **filtered through maple charcoal** before it goes into the barrel.
read.mixup: **Bourbon** and **rye** are both American. The grain is the difference: corn is sweeter, rye is spicier.
read.sayIt: Bourbon is a little sweeter; rye is a little spicier.

keyPoints.line: Scotch is made and aged there, at least three years.
is malted barley from one distillery.
mixes malt and grain whisky: most Scotch sold.
many are peated, so they taste smoky.

read.where: **Scotch** is whisky made in **Scotland** and aged there at least **three years** in oak. An age on the label is the **youngest** whisky in the bottle. **Single malt** is 100% malted barley from **one distillery**. **Blended Scotch** mixes malt and grain whiskies; it’s most of the Scotch sold. Many **Islay** whiskies are **peated**: the malt is dried over a peat fire, which makes them **smoky**.

read.bigIdea: Three more you’ll see on the back bar.
read.where: **Irish whiskey** is made on the island of **Ireland** and aged at least **three years** in wood. **Single pot still**, made from malted and unmalted barley, is unique to Ireland: creamy and spicy. Most Irish whiskey sold is **blended**. **Japanese whisky** has a makers’ standard from **2021**: made with Japanese water, aged at least three years and bottled, all in **Japan**. On a **Canadian** label, “rye” and “Canadian whisky” mean the same thing.

read.bigIdea: Neat, on the rocks, or with a mixer.
read.where: Many guests sip whiskey **neat** or **on the rocks**, and some like a **splash of water**. Mixed, the common calls are **whiskey and ginger ale**, **whiskey and soda** and **whiskey and cola**. Ask **which whiskey**: bourbon, rye and Scotch taste very different. If the guest names the bottle, it’s a **call**.

stops.name: With water
stops.text: A **splash** of water, if they ask.

read.mixup: **Neat** never touches ice. **Up** is chilled on ice, but the ice stays in the tin.
read.sayIt: Bourbon, rye or Scotch? And neat or on the rocks?

read.where: The **Old Fashioned** is bourbon or rye, sugar and bitters. The **Manhattan** is rye, sweet vermouth and bitters. The **Whiskey Sour** is bourbon, lemon and sugar, sometimes with **egg white**. The **Sazerac** is rye with Peychaud’s bitters and an absinthe rinse. The **Penicillin** is blended Scotch, lemon and honey-ginger, with Islay on top. **Irish Coffee** is Irish whiskey, hot coffee, sugar and cream.
read.mixup: A **Manhattan** made with **Scotch** is a **Rob Roy**.
read.sayIt: It’s whiskey-forward: rich, a little sweet, and strong.

facts.fact: Whiskey is distilled from a grain mash and aged in oak. The grain sets the style: corn, rye, wheat or malted barley. Time in the barrel adds color and flavors like vanilla and spice, and softens the spirit. In the US, whiskey is bottled at 80 proof or more.
facts.source: US TTB standards of identity, 27 CFR 5.143 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/27/5.143); Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 (legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2009/2890)

facts.fact: Bourbon is American whiskey of at least 51% corn, aged in new charred oak. It can be made anywhere in the US, not only Kentucky. Corn makes it rounder and sweeter: vanilla and caramel. Rye whiskey is at least 51% rye, so it’s drier and spicier. Wheated bourbons swap rye for wheat and taste softer. Tennessee whiskey, like Jack Daniel’s, follows the bourbon rules and is filtered through maple charcoal before it goes into the barrel.
facts.source: US TTB standards of identity, 27 CFR 5.143 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/27/5.143); Tennessee House Bill 1084 (2013)

facts.fact: Scotch is whisky made in Scotland and aged there at least three years in oak. An age on the label is the youngest whisky in the bottle. Single malt is 100% malted barley from one distillery. Blended Scotch mixes malt and grain whiskies; it’s most of the Scotch sold. Many Islay whiskies are peated: the malt is dried over a peat fire, which makes them smoky.

Irish whiskey is made on the island of Ireland and aged at least three years in wood. Single pot still, made from malted and unmalted barley, is unique to Ireland: creamy and spicy. Most Irish whiskey sold is blended. Japanese whisky has a makers’ standard from 2021: made with Japanese water, aged at least three years and bottled, all in Japan. On a Canadian label, “rye” and “Canadian whisky” mean the same thing.
facts.source: Irish Whiskey Technical File (2014); Japan Spirits & Liqueur Makers Association, Standards for Labeling Japanese Whisky (2021), as summarized by Nikka (nikka.com); Canada Food and Drug Regulations, Canadian whisky (as summarized on Wikipedia)

facts.fact: Many guests sip whiskey neat or on the rocks, and some like a splash of water. Mixed, the common calls are whiskey and ginger ale, whiskey and soda and whiskey and cola. Ask which whiskey: bourbon, rye and Scotch taste very different. If the guest names the bottle, it’s a call.

The Old Fashioned is bourbon or rye, sugar and bitters. The Manhattan is rye, sweet vermouth and bitters. The Whiskey Sour is bourbon, lemon and sugar, sometimes with egg white. The Sazerac is rye with Peychaud’s bitters and an absinthe rinse. The Penicillin is blended Scotch, lemon and honey-ginger, with Islay on top. Irish Coffee is Irish whiskey, hot coffee, sugar and cream.
